name: facade
intent: Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
problem: Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
context: Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
benefits: Shields clients from subsystem internals: a dependency on many classes collapses to one entry type, so client code stays small and stable.

Loose coupling: the subsystem can be refactored, upgraded or replaced behind the facade, and in compiled languages the facade can cut compilation dependencies by keeping subsystem headers/imports out of the client's view.
Centralizes orchestration rules - call order, defaults, validation, error translation and resource lifecycle - in one place instead of duplicating them in every caller.
Creates a natural seam for cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, retries, transactions) and for testing the workflow as a unit rather than re-testing the wiring everywhere.
Enables layering: each layer exposes a facade as its entry point, so layer-to-layer traffic goes through stable, coarse-grained interfaces that are also friendlier to remote boundaries.
Provides a first-party API entry point for third-party consumers (library users, external teams, partner integrations) that does not expose internal type churn.
Enables independent subsystem evolution: subsystem changes that do not alter the facade's observable contract require no client changes.
tradeoffs: The facade is a change magnet: every new subsystem capability tempts another method, and an unbounded facade ends up as complex as the subsystem it was meant to hide.
It exposes only the common subset of the subsystem; capabilities are lost to callers unless the entry point keeps an escape hatch, and a facade that hides too much is simply bypassed.
It adds a layer that must be maintained and debugged: one more indirection in stack traces and profiles, and one more API whose documentation can drift from the subsystem it fronts.

The pattern cannot prevent bypass: nothing stops clients from importing subsystem classes, so without mechanical access control (packages, modules, internal/ directories, access levels) the boundary erodes.
Domain or business logic tends to leak into the facade, turning an orchestration seam into a second, competing home for rules that belong in the subsystem.
Testability is not automatic: a facade that constructs concrete collaborators internally cannot be tested in isolation, and a facade that accepts them concedes part of its simplicity.
Coarse-grained operations can degenerate into god queries or god writes, and the extra layer can obscure where time is actually spent.

In compiled languages, the facade can become a compilation bottleneck: a change to the facade header triggers rebuilds of every client, and facade source-control contention slows teams in parallel development.
Concurrent execution of independent subsystem calls can introduce race conditions or deadlock if the facade does not reason about thread-safety of subsystem objects.

participants.responsibility: Knows which subsystem classes handle a request, exposes a coarse-grained interface for the tasks clients actually perform, and delegates each request to the right collaborators (optionally initializing, validating, translating errors and managing their lifecycle).
Implement the functionality, do the actual work assigned by the facade, and are never aware of the facade - they accept it as just another client and keep operating with each other directly.
Calls the subsystem only through the facade's interface, depending on one entry point rather than on subsystem types and call sequences.

use_cases: Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.

JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.

Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.

Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.

Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.

API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.

SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.

SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.

Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.

jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.
avoid_when: Only one or two classes are involved and their API is already stable: calling them directly keeps the dependency honest and saves a layer.
Clients genuinely need the full subsystem surface - the facade becomes a transparent one-to-one forwarding wrapper (not a facade) or is constantly bypassed.
The subsystem is already a single cohesive module with a small, task-oriented API: that module is itself the entry interface, and a facade would be a rename.
The real problem is an incompatible interface rather than a complicated one: Adapter's interface conversion is the smaller, correct fix.
The intended 'facade' would contain the shared business rules that several clients must vary: that is a domain service or Mediator, and putting it in a facade duplicates the domain.
A single call site exists: an inline helper already keeps orchestration in one place.
The subsystem is a single heavy object where Proxy's lazy-loading, access control or remote-proxy semantics are the actual need.
anti_patterns: God facade: dozens of unrelated methods accumulate until the facade is as complex as the subsystem, becoming the coupling point it was supposed to remove.
One-to-one forwarding wrapper: every facade method mirrors exactly one subsystem call, adding indirection but no simplification.
Static/global singleton facade used everywhere: it becomes a service locator, hides dependencies and defeats substitution in tests.
Business-logic facade: domain rules and transaction policy migrate into the facade, duplicating the subsystem's model and blurring the layer boundary.
Exception-swallowing facade: hiding complexity is taken to mean hiding failures, so callers cannot detect or compensate for errors.
Documentary boundary: the facade exists but clients keep importing subsystem internals, so the entry point is bypassed and the coupling returns.

Tight-facade coupling (industrial pitfall): facade methods are signatures that expose subsystem return types or exceptions, so every internal change forces a facade change and a client rebuild — the facade becomes a compilation bottleneck rather than an insulator.
Leaky-abstraction facade: returning raw subsystem entities or exposing subsystem-specific error types in the public interface re-couples callers to internals the facade was meant to hide.

Shared BFF bottleneck: multiple client teams share one BFF facade, causing cross-team coordination for every client-specific change and reproducing the monolith bottleneck the pattern was meant to eliminate.

Anti-corruption layer erosion: the facade translating between bounded contexts starts accepting domain concepts from the external system, polluting the internal model — the corruption migrates through the facade boundary.
design_principles: Encapsulation and information hiding: expose intent, hide the parts.
Low coupling / Law of Demeter: a client should talk to one neighbour, not to a graph of subsystem objects.
Single responsibility: the facade coordinates and delegates; it does not own domain rules.
Interface segregation: publish a narrow, task-oriented interface rather than the subsystem's full surface.
Dependency inversion: clients and subsystems meet at an abstraction, so alternate subsystem implementations can sit behind the same entry point.
Stable Abstraction Principle: the facade should be stable (fewer reasons to change) while the subsystem it wraps is free to evolve.
Principle of least knowledge: a facade embodies the Law of Demeter at the subsystem boundary — clients know only the facade, not the collaborators behind it.
best_practices: Design the facade from the clients' use cases (task-level, coarse-grained operations), never by mirroring subsystem methods.
Inject subsystem collaborators instead of constructing them inside, so the facade is configurable and testable.
Enforce the boundary mechanically where the language allows: exported modules/packages, Go internal/, Rust pub(crate), Swift access levels, C# internal, C static/opaque types, explicit TS re-exports.
Keep the facade free of domain logic — orchestrate, validate at the boundary, translate errors, and own resources deliberately.
Keep an escape hatch for advanced callers (expose the subsystem or a lower-level API) instead of pretending capabilities do not exist.
Decide and document the lifecycle explicitly: does the facade create, own and dispose subsystem objects, or receive them ready-made?
When the facade fronts a library, treat it as published API: version it, document it and keep its signatures stable as the subsystem churns behind it.

Test the orchestration logic — verify the correct sequence of subsystem calls and that short-circuiting on failure prevents downstream calls. Do not test the subsystem's own behavior through the facade.
Use a narrow interface per test scenario: inject mocks only for the subsystem roles the facade actually calls, not for every collaborator the facade happens to know about.
When the facade grows beyond a handful of cohesive operations, split it along subsystem boundaries rather than letting it accumulate unrelated methods — each facade should have one reason to change.
Prefer value-returning facade operations that carry only what callers need (DTOs, receipt objects) over returning raw subsystem objects, which leaks subsystem types into client code.
Return consistent result types from all facade methods — whether using Result<T> patterns, custom result classes, or domain-specific receipt objects — to keep error handling predictable for callers.
Use layered facades (a coarse-grained facade composed of finer-grained facades) to keep each layer's scope bounded and aligned with a single subsystem or client segment.
Integrate circuit breakers at the facade layer to provide graceful degradation when downstream subsystems fail, preventing cascade failures from reaching callers.

When the facade coordinates independent parallel subsystem calls, use async/concurrent patterns carefully: verify subsystem objects are thread-safe, and fail fast on any error to prevent partial state.

In DDD contexts, treat the facade as an Anti-Corruption Layer: translate external system's concepts into domain language at the boundary, and never let external types appear in the facade's return types.

For reactive/event-streaming subsystems, consider exposing Observables, Flows or async generators from the facade rather than blocking calls, allowing consumers to subscribe, batch or debounce events.
Expose facade methods named after business operations (placeOrder, watchMovie, generateReport) rather than technical operations (callServiceA, processData) to align the API with caller intent.

Compose multiple focused facades rather than building one monolithic facade: UserManagementFacade, OrderProcessingFacade and InventoryFacade each serve a distinct client segment and have one axis of change.

related_patterns_notes.adapter: Adapter changes an existing interface to fit what a client expects; Facade creates a new, simpler interface over a subsystem without changing the subsystem's interface. Adapter wraps one object (one-to-one), Facade wraps many (one-to-many). Adapter solves 'I have X but need Y' (interface incompatibility); Facade solves 'this is too complicated' (interface size). Both define a new interface, but Adapter reuses the old one while Facade defines an entirely new one. Facade hides complexity, Adapter reconciles incompatibility.
related_patterns_notes.mediator: Mediator centralizes communication between peer components that know about each other; Facade provides a one-way entry point to a subsystem whose classes do not know the facade exists. In Mediator, colleagues are aware of and reference the mediator; in Facade, subsystem classes are unaware of the facade. Mediator adds communication logic; Facade does not add functionality — it only orchestrates existing calls. Mediator centralizes arbitrary communication; Facade simplifies a known workflow. Use Mediator when objects tightly couple each other; use Facade when clients need simplification.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: Proxy provides a surrogate with the same interface as the target (same IS-A relationship), controlling access (lazy-loading, access control, remote). Facade provides a new, task-oriented interface (different IS-A), not the same interface as the subsystem. Both buffer a complex entity and may initialize it on their own, but Proxy is interchangeable with its subject while Facade is not. Proxy solves 'control access to an object'; Facade solves 'simplify a complex subsystem'.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Decorator attaches responsibilities to an object at runtime without changing its interface (same IS-A), enabling recursive composition; Facade presents a coarse entry point to an entire subsystem and is not primarily about extending individual object behavior. Decorator adds behaviour to one object's interface; Facade simplifies access to many collaborating classes. Decorator's wrapped object has the same interface; Facade's wrapped objects each have their own distinct interfaces.
related_patterns_notes.delegation: Delegation is the general mechanic of forwarding a request; Facade uses delegation intentionally to hide subsystem complexity behind a task-oriented interface. Delegation alone is not a pattern — it is the implementation technique both Facade and Mediator use.
related_patterns_notes.abstract-factory: Abstract Factory produces families of related objects without clients knowing their concrete types; Facade simplifies usage of an already-constructed subsystem. Factories hide 'what concrete classes exist', Facades hide 'how to cooperate with existing classes'. Abstract Factory is creational; Facade is structural. Use Abstract Factory when clients should not know which implementation family they use; use Facade when clients should not know how to coordinate existing implementations.
related_patterns_notes.remote-facade: Remote Facade (Fowler's PEAA) is a specialized Facade variant that exposes a coarse-grained interface over a fine-grained object graph specifically to reduce chattiness in distributed systems. It adds no domain logic and serves purely as a network-level optimizer — it is an application of Facade at the distributed boundary.
related_patterns_notes.session-facade: Session Facade (J2EE/EJB pattern) is a server-side facade that coordinates fine-grained enterprise beans behind a single coarse-grained interface, primarily for transaction management and reducing remote calls across an Enterprise JavaBean layer. It extends the Facade intent with explicit transaction ownership.
related_patterns_notes.wrapper-facade: Wrapper Facade (POSA2) wraps low-level APIs (sockets, threads, synchronization) with type-safe C++ interfaces to simplify resource management and improve portability. It targets C/C++ API gaps, not object-oriented subsystem simplification. Both are Facade applications but Wrapper Facade operates at the systems-programming level.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD) is a Facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system specifically to translate the external model's concepts into domain concepts. The ACL is a Facade with the explicit additional constraint that no external domain concepts may cross the boundary — it actively protects the internal model from corruption, whereas a general Facade may not have a domain-translation responsibility.
related_patterns_notes.backend-for-frontend: Backend for Frontend (BFF) is a specialized Facade in microservices architecture: a thin per-client aggregation service that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client (mobile, web, partner), and handles perimeter concerns. It is a Facade whose subsystem is the microservice mesh and whose client segment is one frontend team. Key distinction: BFF ownership must align with client-team ownership — a shared BFF across client teams is an anti-pattern. The BFF pattern formalizes what general Facade describes structurally. backend-for-frontend
